name: apple-system-mcp
description: Read processes, CPU, memory, network, volumes, open sockets, battery and disk activity on this Mac
long_description:
A local MCP server written in Swift that reads the state of this Mac through the system's own interfaces: libproc and sysctl for processes, Mach for CPU and memory, getifaddrs and the routing sysctl for network interfaces, getfsstat for volumes, IOKit for the battery and storage activity. It uses no third-party code.

system_overview gives the machine as a whole: macOS version and uptime, chip and core layout, CPU use, load average, memory and swap. system_processes lists processes by CPU, memory, name or pid. system_process inspects one pid. system_connections finds which process owns a port. system_network reports interface totals and rates. system_volumes reports free space. system_battery reports the power source and battery. system_disks reports the read and write activity of each drive.

Every percentage and rate, disk rates included, is a measurement between two readings taken sample_ms apart, so those calls take at least that long. CPU % is a percentage of one core.

Every result is bounded too. Processes, sockets, interfaces, volumes, storage drivers and a process's children come one page at a time, and a long command line one window at a time; when a result does not hold everything, its first lines say how much there is and the exact arguments that return the rest (limit and offset, or character_offset and max_characters). A size, a count or a wait outside its range is moved to the nearest allowed value, and the result says which one was used; a pid or a port outside its range is refused.

Every call is bounded: one that has not finished after 30 seconds is abandoned and answered with an error that says so.

The server runs as you, and macOS only lets an ordinary process read the CPU, memory, descriptors and sockets of processes owned by the same user. Other processes are still listed, with their counters shown as n/a. That is a property of the machine, not a fault, and system_status reports the split.

Command-line arguments are returned only on request, because they can contain secrets; values that look like secrets are masked on a best-effort basis. A process's environment is never read.

Nothing is configured, no file contents are read, no network connection is made, and nothing is ever changed, stopped or signalled.

Not affiliated with or endorsed by Apple Inc.

tools.name: system_status
tools.description: Reports that this server is running and how many processes it can see and read. Call it first when a result shows n/a: it tells a limit of this machine from a fault.

tools.name: system_overview
tools.description: The machine as a whole: macOS version and uptime, chip and core layout, CPU use over a short sample, load average, memory, memory pressure and swap. Memory in use is an approximation.

tools.name: system_processes
tools.description: Lists processes one page at a time, the busiest first, with CPU %, memory, threads, owner and name; limit and offset reach the rest, sorted by cpu, memory, name or pid. CPU % is of one core. Counters are readable only for processes of the same user; the rest show n/a.

tools.name: system_process
tools.description: Everything readable about one pid: state, path, owner, parent, start time, CPU rate, memory, threads, disk, descriptors, working directory and a page of its children. Command-line arguments only on request, with likely secrets masked, one window at a time when they are long.

tools.name: system_network
tools.description: Network interfaces, one page at a time, with addresses, 64-bit cumulative byte, packet and error counters, and the current rate in each direction. Totals are per interface, not per process.

tools.name: system_volumes
tools.description: Mounted volumes, one page at a time, with file system, device, total size and the space an ordinary process may use. System-internal volumes are hidden unless requested.

tools.name: system_connections
tools.description: Open TCP and UDP sockets, one page at a time, with addresses, TCP state and the owning process; limit and offset reach the rest. Finds which process listens on a port. Only sockets of the same user's processes are visible.

tools.name: system_battery
tools.description: What the Mac runs on (mains, battery or UPS) and each battery's charge, charging state, time to empty or full, health, temperature and voltage. A desktop answers that it has none. The serial number is never returned.

tools.name: system_disks
tools.description: Read and write activity of each storage driver, one page at a time: bytes and operations since boot, and per second with average latency over a short sample. Named by BSD name, never by model or serial number.
